# 15.3 Theorem GR T21 Algebraic Channel: Hawking Radiation via Quantum Field Theory in Curved Spacetime {#sec:T21-A}

**Claim 15.3.** GR T21 follows from $dx_4/dt = ic$ by the algebraic-symmetry route via Hawking's 1974 calculation: quantum field theory of a free scalar field on the collapsing-star geometry, with Bogoliubov-coefficient analysis of asymptotic particle production.

## 15.3.1 Setup: quantum field on collapsing-star geometry

**Lemma 15.3.1 (Hawking's collapsing-star setup).** Consider a spherically symmetric matter distribution undergoing gravitational collapse to form a Schwarzschild black hole. Quantise a free massless scalar field $\phi(x)$ on this time-dependent background:

(i) Define the "in-vacuum" $|0\rangle_{\mathrm{in}}$ as the state with no particles before the collapse (asymptotic past, $t \to -\infty$, well before horizon formation);
(ii) Define the "out-vacuum" $|0\rangle_{\mathrm{out}}$ as the state with no particles long after the collapse, far from the horizon (asymptotic future, $r \to \infty$);
(iii) Compute the expected number of particles $\langle 0_{\mathrm{in}} | N^{\mathrm{out}}_\omega | 0_{\mathrm{in}} \rangle$ in the out-vacuum, as seen from $|0\rangle_{\mathrm{in}}$.
*Proof.* In two steps.

*Step 1: Hawking 1974 standard setup.* The "in" and "out" Fock spaces are constructed in the asymptotic regions of the spacetime; the time evolution from "in" to "out" through the collapsing-star geometry is implemented by Bogoliubov coefficients $\alpha_{\omega\omega'}, \beta_{\omega\omega'}$ relating the two sets of mode operators.

*Step 2: McGucken-framework structural reading.* The Hawking-radiation calculation traces the *McGucken-Sphere wavefront propagation* of a free massless scalar field through the time-dependent collapsing-star geometry. The McGucken-framework reading: the "in" vacuum state is defined in the asymptotic-past region, where the spacetime is approximately Minkowski (the collapsing source has not yet formed a horizon, and the mass distribution is dispersed); the "out" vacuum state is defined in the asymptotic-future region, far from the formed horizon. The Bogoliubov coefficients are the unitary-evolution amplitudes between these two Fock spaces, computed by the causal-propagation tracing of the field modes through the time-dependent geometry (Lemma 16.2.3 of Chapter 16). The "in" and "out" vacuum states have different particle content because the time-dependent geometry causes positive-frequency modes in the in-asymptotic region to mix with negative-frequency modes in the out-asymptotic region (via the non-zero $\beta$-coefficients). The expected number of particles $\langle 0_{\mathrm{in}} | N^{\mathrm{out}}_\omega | 0_{\mathrm{in}} \rangle$ in the out-vacuum measured from the in-vacuum is what the asymptotic observer detects as Hawking radiation. The structural reading: the Hawking radiation is the *unitary-evolved mode-mixing* of the collapsing-star geometry, with the diagonal content being a thermal Planck spectrum at the Hawking temperature (Theorem 15.3.2 below) and the off-diagonal content carrying the full unitary-evolution information (Lemma 16.2.2 of Chapter 16). $\square$

## 15.3.2 Bogoliubov coefficients and thermal spectrum

**Theorem 15.3.2 (Hawking 1974: Thermal spectrum of out-going radiation).** Computing the Bogoliubov coefficients $\beta_{\omega\omega'}$ via the geometric-optics tracing of out-going modes back to past null infinity through the collapsing star geometry:
(i) The $\beta_{\omega\omega'}$ coefficients are non-zero (vacuum is *not* invariant under in-to-out evolution);
(ii) The integrated mod-squared $\int d\omega' |\beta_{\omega\omega'}|^2$ has the Planck thermal form:
$$\langle N^{\mathrm{out}}_\omega \rangle \;=\; \frac{\Gamma_\omega}{\exp(\hbar \omega/(k_B T_H)) - 1}, \tag{15.3.2.1}$$
with $\Gamma_\omega$ the grey-body factor (frequency-dependent absorption efficiency of the horizon for in-falling modes of frequency $\omega$) and $T_H = \hbar c^3/(8 \pi G M k_B)$ the Hawking temperature.
*Proof.* Hawking's 1974 calculation, [Hawking 1974, 1975]. The key step is the geometric-optics tracing: outgoing modes at future infinity, traced backward through the spacetime to past infinity, undergo exponential redshift in the near-horizon region. This exponential redshift in the geometric-optics phase, combined with the Bogoliubov decomposition of the in-out vacuum mismatch, produces the Planck thermal spectrum with temperature $T_H$.

The full derivation is technical; the standard textbook treatment (Wald §14.3-14.4, Carroll §9.6, Birrell-Davies §8) develops it in detail. The McGucken-framework structural input is that the underlying Wick-rotation $\tau = x_4/c$ (Theorem 4 of the Introduction) supplies the structural justification for the analytic-continuation of the Bogoliubov calculation that arrives at the thermal spectrum. $\square$

## 15.3.3 Hawking luminosity and evaporation timescale

**Corollary 15.3.3 (Hawking luminosity and evaporation timescale).** Integrating the thermal spectrum (15.3.2.1) over frequencies and angular directions, the total emitted power (luminosity) is given by (T21.2):
$$L_H \;=\; \frac{dE}{dt} \;=\; \frac{c^4}{15360 \pi G^2 M^2} \cdot \hbar c^2 \;\sim\; \frac{\hbar c^6}{G^2 M^2}. \tag{T21.2}$$
Equivalently, $dM/dt = -L_H/c^2 \propto -1/M^2$. Integrating: the evaporation timescale from initial mass $M_0$ to zero mass is (T21.3):
$$t_{\mathrm{evap}} \;=\; \frac{5120 \pi G^2 M_0^3}{\hbar c^4} \;\sim\; 10^{67}\,\mathrm{years} \times (M_0/M_\odot)^3. \tag{T21.3}$$

*Proof.* In four steps from the Hawking thermal spectrum and the McGucken-framework reading of the horizon area.

*Step 1: Stefan-Boltzmann integration.* The Hawking thermal spectrum (15.3.2.1) at temperature $T_H = \hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$ (Theorem T21.1) emits black-body radiation from the horizon at the standard rate per unit area. Integrating the Planck distribution over frequencies and angular directions gives the energy-flux density $\sigma T_H^4$ (Stefan-Boltzmann), where $\sigma = \pi^2 k_B^4/(60 \hbar^3 c^2)$. Multiplying by the horizon area $A_H = 4\pi r_s^2 = 16\pi (GM/c^2)^2$:
$$L_H \;=\; \sigma T_H^4 \cdot A_H \;=\; \frac{\pi^2 k_B^4}{60 \hbar^3 c^2} \cdot \frac{\hbar^4 c^{12}}{(8\pi GM k_B)^4} \cdot 16\pi \frac{G^2 M^2}{c^4}.$$
Simplifying the numerical factor: $\pi^2 \cdot 16\pi / (60 \cdot (8\pi)^4) = 1/(15360 \pi^2)$ approximately; with careful tracking of all the factors of $\pi$,
$$L_H \;=\; \frac{\hbar c^6}{15360 \pi G^2 M^2}, \tag{T21.2}$$
which is the Hawking luminosity. The numerical scaling $L_H \propto 1/M^2$ comes from the product $T_H^4 \cdot A_H \propto (1/M)^4 \cdot M^2 = 1/M^2$ — small black holes are *hotter* and *more luminous* (despite their smaller area), with the temperature scaling dominating.

*Step 2: McGucken-framework reading of the area-luminosity scaling.* The horizon area $A_H = 4\pi r_s^2$ is, in the McGucken framework, the area of the McGucken Sphere at the horizon radius $r = r_s$. The Hawking radiation at the universal rate $c$ from this Sphere carries energy outward into the asymptotic region. The luminosity scaling $L_H \propto 1/M^2$ reflects two competing factors: (a) the *area* of the Sphere scales as $r_s^2 \propto M^2$ (more area to radiate from), and (b) the *temperature* of the Sphere scales as $\kappa \propto 1/r_s \propto 1/M$ (smaller-radius Spheres have higher surface-gravity, hence higher Unruh-equivalent temperature). The Stefan-Boltzmann fourth power of the temperature wins: $T_H^4 \cdot A_H \propto (1/M)^4 \cdot M^2 = 1/M^2$.

*Step 3: Mass evolution.* By energy conservation, the black hole loses mass at the rate $dM c^2/dt = -L_H$, equivalently
$$\frac{dM}{dt} \;=\; -\frac{L_H}{c^2} \;=\; -\frac{\hbar}{15360 \pi G^2 M^2 / c^4} \;=\; -\frac{\hbar c^4}{15360 \pi G^2 M^2}.$$
The McGucken-framework reading: the black hole's mass is the spatial-sector content that sources the McGucken-Sphere expansion (curving the spatial geometry); Hawking radiation transports this content outward, with the radiation propagating at universal rate $c$ from the horizon Sphere.

*Step 4: Integration of mass evolution.* Separating variables: $M^2 \, dM = -(\hbar c^4/(15360\pi G^2))\, dt$. Integrating from $M_0$ at $t = 0$ to $0$ at $t = t_{\text{evap}}$:
$$\int_{M_0}^0 M^2 \, dM \;=\; -\frac{\hbar c^4}{15360\pi G^2} t_{\text{evap}},$$
i.e., $-M_0^3/3 = -(\hbar c^4/(15360\pi G^2)) t_{\text{evap}}$, hence
$$t_{\text{evap}} \;=\; \frac{5120 \pi G^2 M_0^3}{\hbar c^4}. \tag{T21.3}$$
For a solar-mass black hole ($M_0 = M_\odot \approx 2 \times 10^{30}$ kg), $t_{\text{evap}} \sim 10^{67}$ years — far longer than the current age of the universe ($\sim 1.4 \times 10^{10}$ years), making Hawking evaporation of stellar-mass black holes a far-future cosmological phenomenon. The McGucken-framework reading: the long evaporation time is the structural consequence of the small Sphere-surface-gravity (low temperature) of macroscopic-area Spheres. $\square$

# 15.4 Theorem GR T21 Geometric Channel: Hawking Temperature from Wick-Rotated $x_4$-Boost at Horizon {#sec:T21-B}

**Claim 15.4.** GR T21 follows from $dx_4/dt = ic$ by the geometric-propagation route via the Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost at the Schwarzschild horizon, exactly as the Unruh temperature was derived for a Rindler observer in §10.7 of Chapter 10.

## 15.4.1 The horizon as a local Rindler horizon

**Lemma 15.4.1 (Near-horizon geometry as Rindler).** In the near-horizon region $r \to r_s$, the Schwarzschild metric reduces to Rindler geometry $\times$ 2-sphere:
$$ds^2 \;\approx\; -\kappa^2\, \rho^2\, dt^2 \;+\; d\rho^2 \;+\; r_s^2\, d\Omega^2, \quad \kappa \equiv \frac{c^3}{4 G M} = \frac{c}{2 r_s}, \tag{15.4.1.1}$$
with $\rho \geq 0$ the proper-distance coordinate from the horizon and $\kappa$ the surface gravity. A static observer at fixed $\rho > 0$ in this near-horizon geometry has proper acceleration $a = \kappa$ towards the horizon (or equivalently, away from infinity in the Rindler coordinate adaptation).
*Proof.* In three steps from the Schwarzschild metric near the horizon and the McGucken-framework reading.

*Step 1: Near-horizon coordinate change.* In the near-horizon region $r \to r_s^+$, introduce the proper-distance coordinate $\rho$ measured from the horizon by integrating $d\rho = dr/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$:
$$\rho \;=\; \int_{r_s}^{r} \frac{dr'}{\sqrt{1 - r_s/r'}} \;\approx\; \int_{r_s}^{r} \sqrt{\frac{r'}{r' - r_s}}\, dr'.$$
At leading order near the horizon, with $r' - r_s$ small, the integrand behaves as $\sqrt{r_s/(r' - r_s)}$, and the integral evaluates to $\rho \approx 2\sqrt{r_s(r - r_s)}$, equivalently $r - r_s \approx \rho^2/(4 r_s)$, hence $r = r_s + \rho^2/(4 r_s)$ for small $\rho$. The corresponding metric components: $1 - r_s/r = (r - r_s)/r \approx (\rho^2/(4 r_s))/r_s = \rho^2/(4 r_s^2) = (\kappa\rho/c)^2$ with $\kappa = c/(2 r_s)$.

*Step 2: Metric in proper-distance coordinates.* The temporal coefficient: $-c^2(1 - r_s/r) \approx -c^2 \cdot \rho^2/(4 r_s^2) = -\kappa^2 \rho^2$. The radial coefficient: $(1 - r_s/r)^{-1} dr^2 \approx (4 r_s^2/\rho^2)(\rho/(2 r_s))^2 d\rho^2 = d\rho^2$ (after the coordinate change $dr \approx (\rho/(2 r_s)) d\rho$ from Step 1). The angular sector is unchanged: $r^2 d\Omega^2 \approx r_s^2 d\Omega^2$ near the horizon. Combining:
$$ds^2 \;\approx\; -\kappa^2 \rho^2\, dt^2 + d\rho^2 + r_s^2\, d\Omega^2,$$
which is Rindler geometry $\times$ 2-sphere with surface gravity $\kappa$.

*Step 3: McGucken-framework structural reading.* The near-horizon Rindler structure is the geometric content of the *coordinate-frame Sphere expansion at the horizon* in the McGucken framework. By Lemma 11.1.3.3 of Chapter 11, the coordinate-frame Sphere-expansion rate at radial coordinate $r$ in the Schwarzschild metric is $c \cdot \sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$. At $r = r_s$, this rate *vanishes* — the coordinate-frame projection of the universal $x_4$-advance rate goes to zero. In the proper-distance coordinate $\rho$, this near-horizon behaviour manifests as the Rindler geometry: the static observer at fixed $\rho > 0$ accelerates with proper acceleration $a = \kappa$ towards the horizon (or equivalently, away from infinity), with the acceleration scaling inversely with $r_s$ (smaller black holes have higher surface gravity). The McGucken-framework reading: at the horizon, the McGucken Sphere of the asymptotic observer has shrunk to zero coordinate-extent — the coordinate-frame $x_4$-advance is foreclosed, but the proper-frame $x_4$-advance continues at universal rate $ic$. The Unruh-temperature identification (Theorem 10.7.1) at this proper acceleration $\kappa$ gives the Hawking temperature $T_H = \hbar\kappa/(2\pi c k_B)$. The near-horizon Rindler structure is therefore the local-frame expression of the *foreclosure of coordinate-time $x_4$-advance* at the horizon, while the *proper-frame $x_4$-advance* continues unchanged. $\square$

## 15.4.2 Hawking temperature = Unruh temperature for the surface-gravity acceleration

**Theorem 15.4.2 (Hawking temperature from the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel).** By Theorem 10.7.1 of Chapter 10 (Unruh temperature from McGucken-Wick rotation), a uniformly accelerated observer at proper acceleration $a$ in Rindler coordinates experiences a thermal bath at temperature $T_U = \hbar a/(2\pi c k_B)$. Applied to the near-horizon static observer at surface-gravity acceleration $a = \kappa$, the Hawking temperature is:
$$T_H \;=\; T_U(\kappa) \;=\; \frac{\hbar \kappa}{2 \pi c k_B} \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{2 \pi c k_B} \cdot \frac{c}{2 r_s} \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{4 \pi k_B r_s} \;=\; \frac{\hbar c^3}{8 \pi G M k_B}. \tag{T21.1}$$

*Proof.* Direct application of the Unruh-temperature theorem (Theorem 10.7.1 of Chapter 10) to the near-horizon static observer.

The structural reading: the Hawking temperature is the *asymptotic-frame* (Tolman-redshifted) Unruh temperature for the surface-gravity acceleration at the horizon. An observer at proper distance $\rho > 0$ from the horizon, accelerated to remain stationary at radial coordinate $r = r_s + \rho^2/(4r_s)$, has local proper acceleration $a_{\mathrm{local}}(r) = (c^2/2)\cdot (r_s/r^2)/\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ towards the horizon, diverging as $r \to r_s^+$. The local Unruh temperature seen by this observer in its own frame is $T_{\mathrm{local}} = \hbar a_{\mathrm{local}}/(2\pi c k_B)$. The Tolman gravitational-redshift relation translates this to the asymptotic observer's frame:
$$T_\infty(r) \;=\; T_{\mathrm{local}}(r) \cdot \sqrt{1 - r_s/r} \;=\; \frac{\hbar c\, r_s}{4\pi k_B\, r^2}.$$
At the horizon ($r = r_s$), this asymptotic temperature is
$$T_\infty(r_s) \;=\; \frac{\hbar c\, r_s}{4\pi k_B\, r_s^2} \;=\; \frac{\hbar c}{4\pi k_B\, r_s} \;=\; T_H,$$
recovering (T21.1). The two derivations (Unruh, Hawking) are *the same derivation* applied to different observers: the Unruh observer is uniformly accelerated in flat spacetime; the Hawking observer is static near a Schwarzschild horizon at surface-gravity acceleration $\kappa = c/(2r_s)$, with the Tolman redshift converting the locally-divergent acceleration into the finite asymptotic Hawking temperature.

The McGucken-framework structural reading: the Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost at the horizon (the same Wick rotation that produces the Unruh temperature in §10.7) produces the Hawking temperature at the surface-gravity acceleration. The Tolman-redshift translation between local and asymptotic frames is the geometric content of the coordinate-frame Sphere-expansion factor $\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ (Lemma 11.1.3.3 of Chapter 11), which vanishes at the horizon (the coordinate-frame $x_4$-advance foreclosed) while the proper-frame $x_4$-advance continues at universal rate $ic$. $\square$

## 15.4.3 Derivation of Hawking's coefficient $\eta = 1/4$ as an output of $dx_4/dt = ic$

The area-law coefficient $\eta$ in $S = \eta\, k_B A_H/\ell_P^2$ was left provisional at Theorem 12 of Chapter 1, where the mode-counting argument fixed the entropy proportional to $A_H/\ell_P^2$ but not its numerical prefactor. We now derive $\eta = 1/4$ as an *output* of the framework. The derivation takes no input from Bekenstein or Hawking: it uses only (i) the Hawking temperature $T_H$, which Theorem 15.4.2 above has just derived from the Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost at the horizon, and (ii) the thermodynamic first law. The coefficient falls out of the integration.

**Theorem 15.4.3 (The area-law coefficient is $1/4$; derived, not matched).** *Let the Hawking temperature be $T_H = \hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$ (Theorem 15.4.2, from the Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost --- no black-hole-thermodynamic input). Let the horizon entropy $S_{\mathrm{BH}}(M)$ be defined thermodynamically by the first law $dE = T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}}$ with $E = Mc^2$, subject to the boundary condition $S_{\mathrm{BH}}(0) = 0$ (no hole, no entropy). Then*
$$S_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; \frac{k_B\, A_H}{4\,\ell_P^{2}}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \eta \;=\; \tfrac14 ,$$
*where $A_H = 4\pi r_s^2$ is the horizon area and $\ell_P^2 = \hbar G/c^3$. The coefficient $1/4$ is an output of $dx_4/dt = ic$, not a constant fixed by matching to a prior result.*

*Proof.* In five steps.

*Step 1 (the first law supplies the entropy differential).* The energy of the hole is $E = Mc^2$, so $dE = c^2\, dM$. The first law $dE = T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}}$ then gives
$$dS_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; \frac{dE}{T_H} \;=\; \frac{c^2\, dM}{T_H}.$$

*Step 2 (insert the independently derived Hawking temperature).* Substituting $T_H = \hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$ from Theorem 15.4.2 --- which was obtained from the McGucken--Wick rotation of the $x_4$-boost at the horizon (Theorem 10.7.1 applied at $a = \kappa = c/2r_s$), with no appeal to any prior entropy formula:
$$dS_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; c^2\, dM \cdot \frac{8\pi G M k_B}{\hbar c^3} \;=\; \frac{8\pi G\, k_B}{\hbar c}\; M\, dM .$$

*Step 3 (integrate, with the boundary condition).* Integrating from $M' = 0$ to $M' = M$, using $S_{\mathrm{BH}}(0) = 0$:
$$S_{\mathrm{BH}}(M) \;=\; \frac{8\pi G\, k_B}{\hbar c} \int_0^{M} M'\, dM' \;=\; \frac{8\pi G\, k_B}{\hbar c} \cdot \frac{M^2}{2} \;=\; \frac{4\pi G\, k_B\, M^2}{\hbar c}. \tag{15.4.3.1}$$
The entropy is thus fixed as a function of mass, with no free constant remaining: the integration constant is killed by the boundary condition, and the prefactor is inherited entirely from $T_H$.

*Step 4 (re-express in terms of horizon area).* The Schwarzschild horizon has radius $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ (GR T12), hence area
$$A_H \;=\; 4\pi r_s^2 \;=\; 4\pi\!\left(\frac{2GM}{c^2}\right)^{\!2} \;=\; \frac{16\pi G^2 M^2}{c^4}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad M^2 \;=\; \frac{A_H\, c^4}{16\pi G^2}.$$
Substituting into (15.4.3.1):
$$S_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; \frac{4\pi G\, k_B}{\hbar c}\cdot \frac{A_H\, c^4}{16\pi G^2} \;=\; \frac{k_B\, A_H\, c^3}{4\,\hbar G}.$$

*Step 5 (read off the coefficient in Planck units).* With $\ell_P^2 = \hbar G/c^3$, so that $c^3/(\hbar G) = 1/\ell_P^2$:
$$\boxed{\;S_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; \frac{k_B\, A_H}{4\,\ell_P^{2}}\;}$$
The numerical coefficient is $\tfrac14$. It was nowhere inserted: it arose as the product of the factor $\tfrac12$ from integrating $M\,dM$ in Step 3 against the geometric factors carried by $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ in Step 4. Hence $\eta = 1/4$ is an output. $\square$

**Remark 15.4.3.1 (what makes this a derivation and not a matching).** The force of Theorem 15.4.3 rests on the *provenance* of the two inputs it uses, and it is worth stating explicitly where each came from, since a circular version of this argument is easy to write by accident.

\begin{itemize}
\item The Hawking temperature $T_H$ is **not** taken from Hawking's 1974 calculation. It is derived at Theorem 15.4.2 from the McGucken--Wick rotation of the $x_4$-boost at the horizon --- the same rotation, and the same $2\pi$ from single-valuedness of the Euclidean $x_4$-circle, that produced the Unruh temperature at Theorem 10.7.1 --- applied at the surface-gravity acceleration $\kappa = c/2r_s$. Every ingredient of $T_H$ is a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$.
\item The horizon radius $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild solution of GR T12, itself a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ along both channels (Chapter 11).
\item The first law $dE = T\,dS$ is the thermodynamic definition of entropy and introduces no black-hole-specific content.
\end{itemize}

*No Bekenstein--Hawking entropy formula is used as an input at any step.* The chain runs $dx_4/dt = ic \Rightarrow$ Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost $\Rightarrow T_H \Rightarrow$ (first law, integrate) $\Rightarrow S_{\mathrm{BH}} = k_B A_H/(4\ell_P^2)$, and the $1/4$ emerges at the end. This is to be contrasted with the *consistency check* of Theorem 15.5.1 below, which starts from $S_{\mathrm{BH}} = k_B A_H/(4\ell_P^2)$ and verifies that $T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}} = dE$ --- a valid check, but one which assumes the coefficient rather than producing it. Theorem 15.4.3 is the derivation; Theorem 15.5.1 is its consistency verification read in the reverse direction.

**Remark 15.4.3.2 (the promissory note of Theorem 12 discharged; and what remains to explain).** Theorem 12 of Chapter 1 established, by $x_4$-mode counting on the horizon McGucken Sphere at the Planck scale, that the horizon entropy is proportional to $A_H/\ell_P^2$ --- one mode per Planck-area cell --- and deferred the numerical coefficient. Theorem 15.4.3 supplies it. The two results are complementary and their combination is the full content of GR T20: *mode-counting on the horizon Sphere gives the area law's form; the Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost, through the Hawking temperature and the first law, gives its coefficient.* Both descend from $dx_4/dt = ic$; neither imports the Bekenstein--Hawking formula.

One thing, however, Theorem 15.4.3 does *not* supply: the *reason* the coefficient is one-quarter rather than some other fraction. The number arrives at the end of an integration, forced at every step yet geometrically opaque. That question --- ``why exactly $1/4$?'' --- is answered at Theorem 15.4.4 of §15.4.4 immediately below, where the coefficient is exhibited as the image of a one-half in the Gibbons--Hawking--York boundary action of the Ricci-flat Euclidean Schwarzschild manifold. Theorem 15.4.3 gives the value; Theorem 15.4.4 gives the reason.

## 15.4.4 Why Euclidean methods work at all: the Wick rotation as the collapse of $x_4$'s perpendicularity

Theorem 15.4.4 below computes an entropy from a Euclidean action. That computation is only as good as the standing of the Euclidean manifold on which it is performed, and in the orthodox treatment that standing is poor. The present subsection supplies it. What follows is the resolution of a recognised open problem --- *why do Euclidean methods work?* --- and it is the enabling structure for everything in §15.4.4 and §15.4.5.

### 15.4.4.1 The orthodox difficulty

In standard quantum field theory the Wick rotation is the substitution $t \mapsto -i\tau$. Under it:

\begin{itemize}
\item the Minkowski line element $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$ becomes the Euclidean $ds_E^2 = c^2d\tau^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2$;
\item Lorentzian oscillating phases $e^{iS/\hbar}$ become Euclidean decaying weights $e^{-S_E/\hbar}$;
\item the Feynman path integral $\int \mathcal{D}\varphi\, e^{iS/\hbar}$ over oscillating amplitudes becomes the Gibbs partition function $Z = \int \mathcal{D}\varphi\, e^{-S_E/\hbar}$ summing Boltzmann weights;
\item quantum mechanics becomes Euclidean statistical mechanics.
\end{itemize}

The device is computationally powerful --- integrals that diverge in Lorentzian signature converge in Euclidean --- and it reproduces the Hawking temperature with remarkable efficiency: Wick-rotate Schwarzschild, impose regularity at the horizon by periodic identification of Euclidean time with period $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$, and read off $T_H = \hbar\kappa/(2\pi c k_B)$. Yet in standard treatments the rotation is a *formal computational trick*, and its success has no first-principles justification. What is ``imaginary time''? Why should a periodic identification in it be a *temperature*? Why does the prescription work at all? Absent an answer, an entropy computed from a Euclidean action is an entropy computed on a device of uncertain physical standing.

### 15.4.4.2 The McGucken reading: the rotation removes the $i$ from $x_4$

**Theorem 15.4.4-0 (The Wick rotation is the collapse of $x_4$'s perpendicularity).** *Under the McGucken Principle, $x_4 = ict$, where the $i$ records $x_4$'s physical perpendicularity to the three spatial coordinates (Theorem 4; Lemma 5.1.2.2). The Wick rotation $t \mapsto -i\tau$ therefore acts on the fourth coordinate as*
$$x_4 \;=\; ict \;\longmapsto\; ic\,(-i\tau) \;=\; c\,\tau .$$
*That is: **the Wick rotation removes the $i$ from $x_4$.** The Euclidean ``imaginary time'' $\tau$ is not imaginary and is not a formal device: it is the real, spatial-like coordinate that $x_4$ becomes when its perpendicularity is removed. The Euclidean geometry is the geometry that would obtain if $x_4$ were **aligned with** --- rather than **perpendicular to** --- the three spatial dimensions. The rotation collapses the four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold (three spatial $+$ one perpendicular $x_4$) onto a four-dimensional Euclidean manifold (three spatial $+$ one aligned $\tau$).*

*Proof.* Immediate from $x_4 = ict$, the integrated shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$ (Lemma 5.1.2.1), together with the substitution $t = -i\tau$: $x_4 = ic(-i\tau) = -i^2 c\tau = c\tau$. The imaginary unit, which by Lemma 5.1.2.2 and Remark 5.1.2.3 is precisely the algebraic record of $x_4$'s perpendicularity to $\Sigma_t$ --- it is what supplies the single minus sign of the Lorentzian signature through $(ic)^2 = -c^2$ --- is exactly what the substitution cancels. Removing it leaves a fourth coordinate $c\tau$ entering the quadratic form with the *same* sign as the three spatial coordinates: the signature becomes $(+,+,+,+)$ and the fourth axis is no longer perpendicular in the Lorentzian sense but aligned with the spatial three. $\square$

**Corollary 15.4.4-1 (every consequence of the rotation follows from the collapse).** Each standard feature of the Wick rotation is a consequence of the perpendicularity-collapse of Theorem 15.4.4-0, and acquires a physical reading thereby:

\begin{itemize}
\item *Oscillating phases become decaying weights.* $e^{iS/\hbar} \mapsto e^{-S_E/\hbar}$ because the $i$ that marked $x_4$'s perpendicularity has been removed, converting $x_4$-oscillations into $\tau$-dampings. The phase oscillated *because* the advance was perpendicular; collapse the perpendicularity and the oscillation becomes a decay.
\item *Quantum mechanics becomes statistical mechanics.* The quantum-mechanical sum over $x_4$-oscillation histories becomes the statistical-mechanical sum over thermal configurations when the $i$ is removed --- the same sum, read on the collapsed geometry.
\item *The $+i\epsilon$ prescription becomes Euclidean regularisation.* The $i$ that selects causal (forward-in-$x_4$) propagation is collapsed onto the real axis, and the causal prescription becomes the Euclidean convergence factor.
\end{itemize}

*The McGucken--Wick rotation is therefore not a formal trick but a physical transformation --- the collapse of $x_4$'s perpendicularity --- and every property of the Euclidean geometry so obtained is a physical property of the collapsed geometry, not a mathematical artifact.* This is the resolution of the orthodox difficulty of §15.4.4.1, and it is what licenses the computations of §15.4.5.

### 15.4.4.3 The near-horizon Euclidean geometry: the cigar

**Theorem 15.4.4-2 (The horizon is the tip of a smooth Euclidean cigar, with angular period $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$).** *Near a non-extremal horizon the Schwarzschild metric takes the Rindler form (Lemma 15.4.1)*
$$ds^2 \;=\; -\kappa^2\rho^2\, dt^2 \;+\; d\rho^2 \;+\; r_s^2\, d\Omega^2 ,$$
*with $\rho$ the proper distance from the horizon and $\kappa = c^4/(4GM)$ the surface gravity. Applying the McGucken--Wick rotation of Theorem 15.4.4-0 --- removing the $i$ from $x_4$ --- gives*
$$ds_E^2 \;=\; \kappa^2\rho^2\, d\tau^2 \;+\; d\rho^2 \;+\; r_s^2\, d\Omega^2 \;=\; \rho^2\, d\theta^2 \;+\; d\rho^2 \;+\; r_s^2\, d\Omega^2, \qquad \theta \equiv \kappa\tau/c ,$$
*which in the $(\rho,\theta)$ sector is **flat polar coordinates on a plane**. Regularity at $\rho = 0$ --- the absence of a conical singularity at the horizon --- requires the angular variable to have the full range $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$, and this forces the periodic identification of Euclidean time with period*
$$\beta \;=\; \frac{2\pi}{\kappa} .$$
*The resulting geometry is the **cigar**: a smooth disk in the $(\rho, \theta)$ sector, opening away from $\rho = 0$, times the transverse $2$-sphere. **The horizon is the tip of the cigar.***

*Proof.* The rotation is Theorem 15.4.4-0 applied to the near-horizon form. The identification $\theta = \kappa\tau/c$ turns the $(\rho,\tau)$ sector into $\rho^2 d\theta^2 + d\rho^2$, the flat plane in polar coordinates. A plane in polar coordinates is smooth at the origin if and only if the angular coordinate runs over exactly $2\pi$; any other range leaves a conical defect at $\rho = 0$, at which the curvature is a delta function and the manifold is singular. Since the Euclidean section is *real geometry* by Theorem 15.4.4-0 --- not a formal continuation whose singularities might be dismissed as artefacts --- a conical singularity at the horizon would be a genuine curvature singularity of the collapsed manifold, which the smooth Schwarzschild exterior does not possess. Hence $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$, i.e. $\kappa\tau/c$ has period $2\pi$, i.e. $\tau$ has period $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$ (in units where $c$ is absorbed into $\tau$). $\square$

**Corollary 15.4.4-3 (the Hawking temperature is the inverse of the cigar's angular period).** In Euclidean field theory, periodic identification of Euclidean time with period $\beta$ *is* thermal equilibrium at temperature $T = \hbar/(k_B\beta)$. Applying this to the cigar of Theorem 15.4.4-2:
$$T_H \;=\; \frac{\hbar}{k_B \beta} \;=\; \frac{\hbar \kappa}{2\pi c\, k_B},$$
which is the Hawking temperature (T21.1), recovered here as a *geometric statement about the cigar's angular period*. This is the same $2\pi$ that appears in the Unruh temperature (Theorem 10.7.1) and in the KMS periodicity of Theorem 13 of §1.5.2; in each case it is the single-valuedness of the Euclidean $x_4$-circle, and it is now visible as the smoothness of a real geometry rather than as a convention.

**Remark 15.4.4-4 (what has been resolved).** The orthodox difficulty of §15.4.4.1 is answered in full. *Why does the Euclidean prescription work?* Because the Euclidean section is not an analytic fiction but the actual geometry of the McGucken manifold with $x_4$'s perpendicularity collapsed. *What is the physical meaning of the periodic identification?* It is the smoothness of that real geometry at the tip of the cigar --- a conical defect at the horizon would be a genuine curvature singularity, and its absence *forces* the period. *Why is a periodicity a temperature?* Because the collapse of the $i$ converts the sum over $x_4$-oscillation histories into the sum over thermal configurations (Corollary 15.4.4-1). Every step is a statement about geometry. The Gibbons--Hawking--York computation of §15.4.5 below is therefore performed on a manifold of established physical standing, and the entropy it yields is a property of that manifold rather than an output of a formal manoeuvre.

## 15.4.5 Why *exactly* one-quarter? The coefficient from the Euclidean action of the McGucken cigar

Theorem 15.4.3 establishes that $\eta = 1/4$ and does so without circularity. But it does not explain *why* the fraction is one-quarter rather than some other number. In that derivation the coefficient arrives at the end of an integration --- the $\tfrac12$ of $\int M\,dM$ against the geometric factors of $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ --- and while every step is forced, the *geometric origin* of the number is not transparent. The question ``why exactly $1/4$?'' is a recognised open problem of black-hole thermodynamics, and the McGucken framework answers it. The answer is that the $1/4$ of the area law is the image of a $\tfrac12$ in the Euclidean gravitational action, and that $\tfrac12$ is a boundary term.

**Theorem 15.4.5 (The coefficient $1/4$ from the Euclidean action of the Schwarzschild cigar).** *Apply the McGucken--Wick rotation (Theorem 4 of the Introduction) to the Schwarzschild exterior. The resulting Euclidean manifold --- the* cigar *near the horizon, smoothly joined to asymptotically Euclidean four-space --- carries total Euclidean gravitational action*
$$I_E \;=\; \tfrac12\,\beta\, M c^2 ,$$
*with $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$ the Euclidean-time period forced by smoothness at the horizon. The partition-function relation $S = k_B\,(\beta \langle E\rangle - I_E/\hbar)$ then yields*
$$S_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; \frac{k_B\, A_H}{4\,\ell_P^{2}} .$$
*The $1/4$ of the area law is the numerical factor $\tfrac12$ of $I_E = \tfrac12\beta M c^2$, carried through to the area. Its geometric origin is the Gibbons--Hawking--York boundary term with the flat-space subtraction.*

*Proof.* In four steps.

*Step 1 (the Euclidean section is real geometry --- established, not assumed).* This step is no longer an assertion. By **Theorem 15.4.4-0**, the McGucken--Wick rotation *removes the $i$ from $x_4 = ict$*, and the Euclidean section is therefore the actual geometry of the McGucken manifold with $x_4$'s perpendicularity collapsed --- three spatial dimensions plus one *aligned* $\tau$, rather than three spatial plus one *perpendicular* $x_4$. It is not ``imaginary time'' and not an analytic continuation of uncertain standing. Applying this rotation to the Schwarzschild exterior gives
$$ds^2_E \;=\; \Bigl(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\Bigr)c^2 d\tau^2 \;+\; \Bigl(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\Bigr)^{-1} dr^2 \;+\; r^2 d\Omega^2 ,$$
and by **Theorem 15.4.4-2** the near-horizon region is the *cigar*: flat polar coordinates in the $(\rho,\theta)$ sector, whose smoothness at the tip --- the absence of a conical curvature singularity at the horizon of a real manifold --- *forces*
$$\beta \;=\; \frac{2\pi}{\kappa}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{c^4}{4GM} .$$
The horizon is the tip of the cigar; far from it the geometry approaches Euclidean four-space. This is the same $2\pi$ that single-valuedness of the Euclidean $x_4$-circle supplied at Theorem 13 of §1.5.2 and at Theorem 10.7.1 (the Unruh temperature), now seen as the smoothness of a geometry rather than as a convention. This is the step at which the framework does work the orthodox treatment cannot (Remark 15.4.4-4): in standard general relativity the Euclidean continuation is a formal manoeuvre whose physical status is obscure, and computing an *entropy* from its action is correspondingly hard to justify. Here the manifold is real, so the computation below is a statement about geometry.

*Step 2 (the Euclidean action, with its boundary term).* The Euclidean gravitational action on a manifold $\mathcal M$ with boundary is
$$I_E \;=\; -\frac{c^3}{16\pi G}\int_{\mathcal M} d^4x\, \sqrt{g}\, R \;-\; \frac{c^3}{8\pi G}\oint_{\partial \mathcal M} d^3x\, \sqrt{h}\,\bigl(K - K_0\bigr),$$
where $K$ is the extrinsic curvature of the boundary and $K_0$ that of the same surface embedded in flat Euclidean space. The second term is the Gibbons--Hawking--York boundary term. It is not an *ad hoc* addition: it is required for the variational principle to be well-posed when it is the induced boundary metric, rather than its normal derivative, that is held fixed.

*Step 3 (evaluation: the bulk vanishes, and the boundary gives one-half).* The Schwarzschild solution is a *vacuum* solution: $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$, hence $R = 0$. **The bulk Einstein--Hilbert integral therefore vanishes identically**, and the *entire* Euclidean action is the boundary term at spatial infinity. Explicit evaluation of that term gives
$$I_E \;=\; \tfrac12\,\beta\, M c^2 .$$
The factor $\tfrac12$ is a geometric consequence of the subtraction $K - K_0$: the extrinsic curvature of a large sphere in the Schwarzschild geometry differs from its extrinsic curvature in flat space by a term proportional to the mass, and the surface integral of that difference returns exactly half the Euclidean period times the mass-energy. *This computation is standard* (Gibbons--Hawking 1977; York 1972); the framework's contribution is Step 1 --- supplying the physical meaning of the manifold on which it is performed.

*Step 4 (entropy from the partition function).* The Euclidean action determines the partition function by $Z = e^{-I_E/\hbar}$, whence
$$S_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; k_B\Bigl(\beta \langle E\rangle - \frac{I_E}{\hbar}\Bigr) \;=\; k_B\Bigl(\frac{\beta M c^2}{\hbar} - \frac{\beta M c^2}{2\hbar}\Bigr) \;=\; \frac{k_B\,\beta M c^2}{2\hbar}.$$
*The entropy is half of $\beta E$ precisely because the Euclidean action consumed the other half.* Substituting $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa = 8\pi G M/c^3$:
$$S_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; \frac{k_B}{2\hbar}\cdot \frac{8\pi G M}{c^3}\cdot M c^2 \;=\; \frac{4\pi G\, k_B\, M^2}{\hbar c},$$
which is exactly (15.4.3.1). With $A_H = 16\pi G^2M^2/c^4$ and $\ell_P^2 = \hbar G/c^3$ this is $S_{\mathrm{BH}} = k_B A_H/(4\ell_P^2)$, so $\eta = 1/4$. $\square$

**Remark 15.4.5.1 (the answer to ``why exactly one-quarter'').** The coefficient is not a mystery and not a coincidence. It descends from two geometric facts about the Euclidean section of the McGucken manifold, and from nothing else:

\begin{enumerate}
\item *Schwarzschild is Ricci-flat.* The bulk Einstein--Hilbert integral vanishes, so the **entire** gravitational action of the black hole is a boundary term. The entropy of a black hole is, in this precise sense, a *surface* quantity because the volume contribution is identically zero --- which is the deepest available statement of *why* horizon entropy scales with area rather than with volume.
\item *The Gibbons--Hawking--York term, with its flat-space subtraction, evaluates to one-half.* $I_E = \tfrac12 \beta Mc^2$, and the entropy $S = k_B(\beta E - I_E/\hbar)$ is therefore *half* of $\beta E$ --- the action having taken the other half. That $\tfrac12$, carried through the substitution $M^2 \mapsto A_H$, becomes the $\tfrac14$ of the area law.
\end{enumerate}

The relation between the two derivations of the coefficient may now be stated exactly. **Theorem 15.4.3 gives the value; Theorem 15.4.4 gives the reason.** The thermodynamic route integrates the first law against an independently derived $T_H$ and arrives at $1/4$ without circularity, but the number appears at the end of an algebraic manipulation. The Euclidean route exhibits the same number as the image of the one-half in the boundary action of a Ricci-flat manifold. Both descend from $dx_4/dt = ic$: the first through the Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost that fixes $T_H$, the second through the Wick-rotated $x_4$-coordinate that *is* the Euclidean section on which the action is computed. They are two readings of a single rotation.

**Remark 15.4.5.3 (a point on which the geometric origin must be stated carefully).** It is tempting to look for the factor $\tfrac12$ in the *angular* structure of the cigar --- to say that the disk contributes ``half an angular range'' and that this is where the one-half comes from. That reading is not available, and it is worth saying why, since the correct account is more interesting.

By Theorem 15.4.4-2, the Euclidean cigar has the **full** angular range $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$. That is precisely what makes it *smooth*: any *smaller* range would leave a conical defect at $\rho = 0$, i.e. a genuine curvature singularity at the horizon of a real manifold, which the framework forbids. The full $2\pi$ is not a choice but a regularity condition, and it is what fixes $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$ and hence the Hawking temperature. There is no half-disk and no halved angular range anywhere in the construction.

The one-half is therefore *not* angular in origin. It is a **boundary-term** fact: with the bulk Einstein--Hilbert integral annihilated by the Ricci-flatness of Schwarzschild, the entire Euclidean action is the Gibbons--Hawking--York surface integral at infinity, and the flat-space subtraction $K - K_0$ evaluates that integral to exactly half of $\beta M c^2$ (Step 3). The entropy $S = k_B(\beta E - I_E/\hbar)$ is then half of $\beta E$ because the action has taken the other half --- and *that* half, carried through the substitution $M^2 \mapsto A_H$, is the one-quarter of the area law. The $2\pi$ of the cigar fixes the *temperature*; the $\tfrac12$ of the boundary term fixes the *entropy coefficient*. They are different geometric facts about the same Euclidean manifold, and conflating them obscures both.

**Remark 15.4.5.4 (honest accounting of the inputs).** The Gibbons--Hawking--York evaluation of Step 3 is inherited mathematics, standing in the same relation to the framework as the Noether kernel of Theorem 10.3.1.3 and Lovelock's uniqueness theorem of §10.4.1: a computation the framework *employs*, performed on structures the framework *supplies*. What $dx_4/dt = ic$ contributes here is not the surface integral but the manifold --- specifically (i) that the Euclidean section is physically real, being the geometry with $x_4$'s perpendicularity collapsed rather than a formal continuation (Theorem 15.4.4-0); (ii) that the Euclidean period is $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$, forced by the smoothness of that real geometry at the tip of the cigar (Theorem 15.4.4-2), the same single-valuedness of the $x_4$-circle this framework has used since Theorem 13 of §1.5.2; and (iii) that the Schwarzschild geometry on which the computation runs is itself a theorem of the Principle (GR T12). In the orthodox treatment the Euclidean continuation is a device of uncertain standing, and the resulting entropy is correspondingly difficult to interpret; here it is a statement about the actual geometry of a manifold whose fourth dimension is expanding at $ic$. The full development is given in the companion paper [31a] [MG-Hawking], Proposition V.1 (the factor $1/4$ from the Euclidean Einstein--Hilbert action on the Schwarzschild cigar) and §V.3 (Resolution of the open problem HK-3: why exactly one-quarter). What $dx_4/dt = ic$ contributes here is not the surface integral but the manifold --- specifically (i) that the Euclidean section is physically real, being the geometry with the $i$ removed from $x_4 = ict$ rather than a formal continuation; (ii) that the Euclidean period is $\beta = 2\pi/\kappa$, forced by the single-valuedness of the $x_4$-circle that this framework has used since Theorem 13 of §1.5.2; and (iii) that the Schwarzschild geometry on which the computation runs is itself a theorem of the Principle (GR T12). ## 15.4.6 The trans-Planckian problem dissolves: there is nothing below the Planck scale to count

Hawking's derivation carries a difficulty that has never been resolved within the orthodox framework, and that is worth stating plainly before it is dissolved. The calculation traces late-time radiation modes backwards in time to their origin near the horizon, where the exponential blueshift means they had *arbitrarily short* wavelengths --- formally, far below the Planck length. But quantum field theory on curved spacetime has no domain of validity there. **The derivation's prediction therefore depends on the behaviour of modes in a regime where the theory used to derive it does not apply.** Various repairs have been attempted --- modified dispersion relations, holographic ultraviolet completions --- and no consensus exists.

In the McGucken framework the problem does not require a repair. It does not arise.

**Theorem 15.4.6 (The trans-Planckian regime is not a physical domain).** *The $x_4$-oscillation is Planck-scale quantised: the fundamental wavelength of $x_4$-advance is $\ell_P$ (Theorem 12 of §1.5.2). Modes of wavelength shorter than $\ell_P$ are therefore **not independent degrees of freedom**; they are the same $x_4$-oscillation state viewed in different frequency windows. The physical mode count on a horizon of area $A$ is bounded:*
$$N_{\mathrm{modes}} \;=\; \frac{A}{\ell_P^2},$$
*one mode per Planck-area cell, and there is nothing below that scale to count. The trans-Planckian ``modes'' appearing in the standard Hawking calculation are not physically distinct; the calculation's formal extension to arbitrarily short wavelengths **double-counts the same physical modes**. Consequently the trans-Planckian regime does not exist as a separate physical domain, and no theory of it is owed.*

*Proof.* The Planck-scale quantisation of the $x_4$-advance is not introduced here for the purpose: it is the *same* fact the framework has already used, and used twice. It is the content of Theorem 12 of §1.5.2, where the fundamental wavelength of $x_4$-advance is identified as $\ell_P = \sqrt{\hbar G/c^3}$ and the number of independent quantum modes of $x_4$-advance crossing a McGucken Sphere of area $A$ is counted as one per Planck-area cell, $N_{\mathrm{modes}} = A/\ell_P^2$ --- the count from which the *form* of the area law descends. A mode of wavelength $\lambda < \ell_P$ would be an $x_4$-oscillation finer than the fundamental $x_4$-wavelength, which is not a distinct oscillation state but the same state re-labelled. The mode count is therefore *bounded above* by $A/\ell_P^2$, exactly.

Hawking's calculation, conducted in a field theory that admits modes of arbitrarily short wavelength, has no such bound and traces the outgoing modes back through wavelengths $\lambda \ll \ell_P$. Those traced-back configurations are not additional physical modes on the McGucken manifold; they are the *same* $A/\ell_P^2$ modes, re-expressed in frequency windows the underlying oscillation does not resolve. The extension is formal, not physical, and it double-counts. Hence the trans-Planckian regime, in which the orthodox derivation is obliged to reason and unable to, is not a region of physics at all. $\square$

**Remark 15.4.6.1 (the area law and the trans-Planckian dissolution are the same fact).** These two results are not neighbours; they are one result read twice. *The horizon has finitely many modes* --- $A/\ell_P^2$ of them --- and from that single fact both consequences follow. Read one way it gives the area law its *form*: entropy proportional to area, one bit per Planck cell, which is why horizon entropy scales with a *surface* (Theorem 12; and see Remark 15.4.5.1, where Ricci-flatness independently makes the entire gravitational action a boundary term). Read the other way it dissolves the trans-Planckian problem: *there is nothing below the Planck scale to count*, so the sub-Planckian modes of the orthodox calculation are bookkeeping, not physics. The orthodox framework has the area law without the bound, and the trans-Planckian problem is the price of that: a mode count that runs to infinity where the physics is finite. The McGucken framework has the bound at the foundation --- the $x_4$-advance has a fundamental wavelength --- and gets both the area law and the absence of the problem from it. *A theory whose modes are counted is a theory that cannot be asked what happens below the counting.*

## 15.4.7 Evaporation: the mass-loss law from $x_4$-stationary-mode emission

**Theorem 15.4.7 (Evaporation rate $dM/dt \propto -1/M^2$).** *The horizon is populated by $x_4$-stationary modes, thermally distributed at $T_H$ (Corollary 15.4.4-3), with mode density one per Planck area (Theorem 12). These modes are carried outward at rate $c$ by the $x_4$-expansion --- the $+ic$ orientation of component (iii), which propagates the wavefront outward and not inward --- and radiate into the exterior. The emitted flux is therefore the blackbody flux at $T_H$,*
$$\frac{dE}{dt} \;=\; -\,\sigma\, A\, T_H^4 ,$$
*and for a Schwarzschild hole, with $T_H \propto 1/M$ (T21.1) and $A \propto M^2$ (GR T12),*
$$\frac{dM}{dt} \;\propto\; -\,M^2 \cdot \frac{1}{M^4} \;=\; -\,\frac{1}{M^2}.$$
*The hole radiates faster as it shrinks, and evaporates in finite time.*

*Proof.* By Corollary 15.4.4-3 the near-horizon field is thermal at $T_H = \hbar\kappa/(2\pi c\,k_B)$ --- established there from the cigar's angular period, with no Bogoliubov input. By Theorem 12 the horizon carries $A/\ell_P^2$ modes, and by Theorem 15.4.6 that count is exact and bounded: the emission is a sum over *finitely many* physical modes, and the Stefan--Boltzmann integral over the thermal spectrum converges without an ultraviolet cut-off imposed by hand. The outward direction of the emission is not an assumption but the $+ic$ orientation: the McGucken Sphere expands from every event of the horizon and does not contract (component (iii)), so the modes are carried *out*. # 15.5 First Law of Black-Hole Thermodynamics and Preview of the Information Paradox

## 15.5.1 The first law: $dE = T\, dS$ at the horizon

**Theorem 15.5.1 (First law of black-hole thermodynamics; consistency verification).** Combining GR T20 and GR T21: a Schwarzschild black hole satisfies the first law of thermodynamics
$$dE \;=\; T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}}, \tag{15.5.1.1}$$
with $E = M c^2$ the rest energy of the hole, $T_H$ the Hawking temperature, and $S_{\mathrm{BH}}$ the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy.

*Logical status.* This theorem *starts from* $S_{\mathrm{BH}} = k_B A_H/(4\ell_P^2)$ and verifies that it is consistent with $T_H$ through the first law. It is therefore a *consistency check*, not the derivation of the coefficient $1/4$: it assumes the factor it would need to produce. The derivation of $1/4$ as an output runs in the opposite direction and is carried out at Theorem 15.4.3 --- from $T_H$ (itself derived from the Wick-rotated $x_4$-boost) through the first law, integrated with $S(0) = 0$, to $S_{\mathrm{BH}}$. The present theorem is that derivation read backwards, and serves as its verification.
*Proof.* In three steps.

*Step 1: Differential of mass-energy.* The Schwarzschild black hole's rest energy is $E = Mc^2$. The differential is
$$dE \;=\; c^2\, dM.$$

*Step 2: Differential of Bekenstein-Hawking entropy.* The Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of Schwarzschild is $S_{\mathrm{BH}} = k_B A_H/(4\ell_P^2)$ with $A_H = 4\pi r_s^2 = 4\pi(2GM/c^2)^2 = 16\pi G^2 M^2/c^4$. Substituting:
$$S_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; \frac{k_B \cdot 16\pi G^2 M^2/c^4}{4\ell_P^2} \;=\; \frac{4\pi k_B G^2 M^2}{c^4 \ell_P^2} \;=\; \frac{4\pi k_B G^2 M^2}{c^4 \cdot \hbar G/c^3} \;=\; \frac{4\pi k_B G M^2}{c \hbar},$$
using $\ell_P^2 = \hbar G/c^3$. Differentiating with respect to $M$:
$$\frac{dS_{\mathrm{BH}}}{dM} \;=\; \frac{8\pi k_B G M}{c \hbar}.$$

*Step 3: First-law identity.* The Hawking temperature of Schwarzschild is $T_H = \hbar c^3/(8\pi G M k_B)$ (Theorem T21.1). The product $T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}}$ for an infinitesimal mass change $dM$:
$$T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}} \;=\; T_H \cdot \frac{dS_{\mathrm{BH}}}{dM}\, dM \;=\; \frac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi G M k_B} \cdot \frac{8\pi k_B G M}{c \hbar}\, dM \;=\; c^2\, dM.$$
Comparing with Step 1: $T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}} = c^2\, dM = dE$, which is the first law (15.5.1.1).

*McGucken-framework structural reading.* The first law $dE = T_H\, dS_{\mathrm{BH}}$ is the thermodynamic identity between the differentials of mass-energy and entropy of the Schwarzschild black hole, with the Hawking temperature as the integrating factor. The McGucken-framework reading: the mass-energy of the hole, by Lemma 11.1.3.3 of Chapter 11, is the spatial-sector content that sources the McGucken-Sphere expansion (curving the spatial geometry); the entropy, by the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel mode-counting of §15.2 (Proposition 15.2.3.1), is the number of $x_4$-stationary modes on the horizon Sphere, scaled by $k_B$ and the Hawking $1/4$ prefactor (Proposition 15.2.4.1). The first law expresses the *equivalence between mass-energy content and horizon-mode count*: adding mass $dM$ to the hole adds $c^2\, dM$ of mass-energy and $dS_{\mathrm{BH}} = c^2\, dM / T_H$ of horizon entropy, with the Hawking temperature being the exact conversion factor between mass-energy and entropy at the McGucken-Sphere horizon. The cross-channel verification: $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel (Euclidean action, §15.1) and the Geometric Channel (mode counting, §15.2) agree on the first law via independent paths. $\square$

The first law is the structural content unifying GR T20 (entropy = area) and GR T21 (temperature from Wick rotation): together they make the black hole a genuine thermodynamic system, obeying the standard thermodynamic identities.

## 15.5.2 The second law: generalised area increase

**Theorem 15.5.2 (Generalised second law of black-hole thermodynamics).** For any process involving black holes and external matter, the *generalised entropy* $S_{\mathrm{gen}} = S_{\mathrm{BH}} + S_{\mathrm{matter}}$ does not decrease:
$$dS_{\mathrm{gen}} \;\geq\; 0. \tag{15.5.2.1}$$

The classical area-increase theorem (Hawking 1971: the total horizon area of a system of black holes is non-decreasing) becomes the *generalised* second law (Bekenstein 1972) when Hawking radiation is included: matter falling into a black hole increases $A_H$ (hence $S_{\mathrm{BH}}$); Hawking-radiated matter decreases $A_H$ but increases $S_{\mathrm{matter}}$, with the total non-decreasing.

The McGucken-framework reading: $S_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is the generalised entropy of $x_4$-advance modes (on the horizon Sphere) plus matter modes (in the bulk). The monotonicity of the Geometric Second Law (Theorem 10.5.1) ensures the non-decrease.

## 15.5.3 Preview of the information paradox (Chapter 16)

The Hawking radiation (GR T21) is *thermal*: it carries no information about the matter that fell into the hole, only the total mass-energy. If the hole evaporates completely (T21.3), the original matter's information appears to be *lost* --- the final state is a featureless thermal radiation bath, regardless of what the initial collapsed matter was.

This is the *black-hole information paradox* (Hawking 1976): unitary quantum mechanics demands information conservation, but evaporation appears to produce information loss. The standard textbook treatments offer four resolutions, all unsatisfactory:

1. **Information is genuinely lost.** Violates unitarity of quantum mechanics.
2. **Information is in the Hawking radiation, in subtle correlations.** Requires non-trivial encoding (firewall paradox, AMPS 2012).
3. **Information remains in a Planck-scale remnant.** Conflicts with the small remnant size and finite entropy.
4. **Information escapes via gravitational tunneling.** Speculative; no first-principles derivation.

Chapter 16 develops the McGucken-framework resolution via the **dual-channel architecture** of $dx_4/dt = ic$: the *unitary* content of the Algebraic Channel (algebraic-symmetry) and the *thermodynamic-monotonic* content of the Geometric Channel (geometric-propagation) live at structurally different levels of the principle, with the "paradox" being a category-error that conflates the two. The detailed resolution is GR T22 of Chapter 16.

The imaginary unit $i$ records the perpendicularity of the temporal direction $x_4$ to the three spatial directions. Stated as the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ of §1.1.

In plain words: every massive particle has a fixed allowance of four-speed equal to $c$, distributed between time-direction advance and spatial-direction motion. A particle at rest spends its whole budget on time-advance ($x_4$-direction at rate $c$); a particle moving spatially at speed $v$ spends part on spatial motion, leaving less for time-advance; a photon spends all of its budget on spatial motion at $c$, with zero time-advance.

This is the formal heart of quantum mechanics, producing the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and forcing quantum states into a Hilbert space rather than a classical phase-space.

- **the McGucken-Invariance Lemma** --- the *McGucken-Invariance Lemma* (Theorem GR T2): the rate $dx_4/dt = ic$ is independent of the spacetime metric, $\partial(dx_4/dt)/\partial g_{\mu\nu} = 0$. # 16.1 The Standard Formulation of the Black-Hole Information Paradox {#sec:paradox}

## 16.1.1 Hawking 1976: the original formulation

Hawking 1976 [Hawking 1976] formulated the paradox as follows. Consider a star of mass $M$ in some pure quantum state $|\psi_{\mathrm{initial}}\rangle$ (a definite quantum state, with all information about the matter fully specified). The star undergoes gravitational collapse to a Schwarzschild black hole, then radiates Hawking radiation (GR T21) until it evaporates completely (T21.3). The final state of the radiation, in Hawking's original treatment, is a *thermal density matrix* $\hat\rho_{\mathrm{thermal}}$ at the time-dependent Hawking temperature $T_H(t)$: a mixed state containing only the total mass-energy of the original star, with no detailed information about $|\psi_{\mathrm{initial}}\rangle$.

The mathematical content: the in-state is *pure*, the out-state is *mixed*. The evolution from pure to mixed is *non-unitary*: pure $\to$ pure is required by unitary quantum mechanics; pure $\to$ mixed implies a non-unitary "super-scattering" matrix $S_{\mathrm{super}}$. Hawking proposed that quantum mechanics must be modified to admit pure $\to$ mixed evolution in the presence of black holes.

**Definition 16.1.1 (The information paradox).** Pure-to-mixed evolution of quantum states under the combined process (gravitational collapse + Hawking evaporation) appears to violate the unitarity of quantum mechanics. Either quantum mechanics is modified, or some currently-unidentified physical mechanism preserves information in the Hawking radiation, or some currently-unidentified part of the spacetime stores the information.

## 16.1.3 The Page curve and the 2019-2020 replica-wormhole calculations

Page 1993 [51] computed the entanglement entropy $S_{\mathrm{ent}}(t)$ between the Hawking radiation and the residual black hole as a function of time during evaporation. For a *unitary* evolution, the entanglement entropy follows the *Page curve*: rising linearly from zero (no radiation, no entanglement) at $t = 0$; reaching a maximum at the Page time $t_{\mathrm{Page}} \approx t_{\mathrm{evap}}/2$ (where the radiation entropy equals the residual hole's entropy); and decreasing linearly back to zero at $t = t_{\mathrm{evap}}$ (complete evaporation, no entanglement because radiation is in a pure state).

For a *non-unitary* evolution (Hawking's original treatment), the entanglement entropy *monotonically* increases throughout evaporation: thermal radiation never decorrelates. The choice between these two curves is the empirical signature distinguishing the unitary and non-unitary scenarios.

In 2019-2020, the *replica-wormhole* calculations (Penington 2019, Almheiri et al. 2020, Penington-Shenker-Stanford-Witten 2019) derived the Page curve from the gravitational path integral, using the saddle-point dominance of replica-wormhole geometries after the Page time. The calculations are consistent with unitarity and establish the Page curve as the correct entanglement-entropy curve, but the *mechanism* by which unitarity is preserved remains structurally unclear in those treatments.

The McGucken-framework resolution of §§16.2--16.5 below provides this structural reading: the Page curve is the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel unitary content; the apparent thermality is the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel coarse-grained content; the replica-wormhole geometries are the Algebraic Channel computational tool for tracking the unitary content through the dual-channel architecture.


# 16.2 Part (a) of GR T22: Algebraic Channel Unitarity via the Bogoliubov S-Matrix {#sec:T22-A}

## 16.2.1 The Bogoliubov transformation as a unitary map

**Lemma 16.2.1 (Bogoliubov transformation is unitary).** The Bogoliubov transformation $\hat U_{\mathrm{Bog}}: \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}} \to \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{out}}$ relating in-Fock-space mode operators to out-Fock-space mode operators is a unitary map between Fock spaces:
$$\hat a^{\mathrm{out}}_\omega \;=\; \sum_{\omega'} \alpha^*_{\omega\omega'}\, \hat a^{\mathrm{in}}_{\omega'} \;+\; \beta^*_{\omega\omega'}\, (\hat a^{\mathrm{in}}_{\omega'})^\dagger, \tag{16.2.1.1}$$
with the Bogoliubov coefficients $\alpha_{\omega\omega'}, \beta_{\omega\omega'}$ satisfying the unitarity constraints
$$\sum_{\omega'} \left(|\alpha_{\omega\omega'}|^2 - |\beta_{\omega\omega'}|^2\right) \;=\; 1, \quad \sum_{\omega'} \left(\alpha_{\omega\omega'} \beta_{\omega'\omega''} - \beta_{\omega\omega'} \alpha_{\omega'\omega''}\right) \;=\; 0. \tag{16.2.1.2}$$

*Proof.* The Bogoliubov transformation must preserve the canonical commutation relations on both Fock spaces:
$$[\hat a^{\mathrm{out}}_\omega, (\hat a^{\mathrm{out}}_{\omega'})^\dagger] = \delta_{\omega\omega'}, \quad [\hat a^{\mathrm{out}}_\omega, \hat a^{\mathrm{out}}_{\omega'}] = 0.$$
Substituting (16.2.1.1) and computing the commutators in terms of $[\hat a^{\mathrm{in}}_{\omega'}, (\hat a^{\mathrm{in}}_{\omega''})^\dagger] = \delta_{\omega'\omega''}$ yields the constraints (16.2.1.2). These are the Bogoliubov-unitarity conditions and are equivalent to the unitarity of the map $\hat U_{\mathrm{Bog}}$ between the in and out Fock spaces.

The full unitarity of $\hat U_{\mathrm{Bog}}$ as a Hilbert-space map (preserving inner products on coherent-state superpositions) follows from the preservation of the canonical commutation relations on the algebra level [65, §3]. The McGucken-framework underwriting: this is the QM T1 of Chapter 25 of the quantum chain (unitary evolution as a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$) applied to the in-to-out evolution; the Bogoliubov transformation is the specific unitary evolution in the collapsing-star background. $\square$

**Lemma 16.2.3 (Bogoliubov coefficients encode causal propagation through collapsing-star geometry).** The Bogoliubov coefficients $\alpha_{\omega\omega'}, \beta_{\omega\omega'}$ are computed by:

## 16.3.4 The refined Generalized Second Law: the same law, a moving partition

The Geometric Channel reading of §16.3.3 asserts that the *total* entropy is non-decreasing while the horizon shrinks. That assertion must be proved, and its proof is the resolution of a long-standing puzzle in black-hole thermodynamics. The classical area theorem --- the statement that the horizon area never decreases --- *fails* under Hawking radiation: the hole evaporates, and $A$ shrinks. Bekenstein and Hawking argued that a *refined* Generalized Second Law nevertheless survives,
$$\frac{dS_{\mathrm{ext}}}{dt} \;+\; \frac{dS_{\mathrm{BH}}}{dt} \;\ge\; 0, \qquad S_{\mathrm{BH}} = \frac{k_B A}{4\ell_P^2},$$
the entropy carried out by the radiation compensating the area loss at every stage. In the orthodox treatment this balance is a *remarkable fact*: it has to be checked, and its mechanistic basis was never identified. Why should the outgoing radiation carry *exactly* enough entropy, at every instant, to cover the shrinking horizon?

In the McGucken framework there is nothing to check. The balance is forced.

**Theorem 16.3.4 (Refined Generalized Second Law from the global McGucken second law).** *Let a black hole evaporate by Hawking emission. Let $S_{\mathrm{ext}}$ denote the entropy of all matter and radiation exterior to the horizon --- now including the Hawking-emitted flux --- and let $S_{\mathrm{BH}} = k_B A/(4\ell_P^2)$ track the horizon. Then*
$$\frac{dS_{\mathrm{ext}}}{dt} \;+\; \frac{dS_{\mathrm{BH}}}{dt} \;\ge\; 0$$
*at every instant of the evaporation. The Generalized Second Law is not a new law and requires no refinement: it is the **global Geometric Second Law of $dx_4/dt = ic$ (Theorem 11 of §1.5.2; Theorem 10.5.1) applied to an evolving partition.** Only the partition changes.*

*Proof.* In three steps.

*Step 1 (the Geometric Second Law holds at every instant, for every process).* By Theorem 11 of §1.5.2, the $+ic$ orientation of the $x_4$-advance --- component (iii) of the Principle: *the fourth dimension advances; it does not retreat* --- gives the strict monotonicity
$$\frac{dS_{\mathrm{total}}}{dt} \;>\; 0$$
for the total entropy of the manifold, at every instant and for *any* physical process. This is not a statistical tendency admitting of exceptions (Theorem 11: the monotonicity is exact, with no Poincaré recurrence, *because $x_4$ does not recur*). Hawking emission is a physical process like any other, and is therefore covered: the emitted quanta are riders of the $x_4$-expansion (Lemma 7.2.3.2), carried outward at rate $c$, and their entropy is bookkept in $S_{\mathrm{total}}$ along with everything else. *No separate law is invoked for the radiation.*

*Step 2 (the partition evolves; the law does not).* The horizon partitions the manifold into an exterior (causally connected to future null infinity) and an interior (causally disconnected). For a *stationary* hole this partition is fixed, and the Geometric Second Law applied across it gives the ordinary Generalized Second Law. For an *evaporating* hole the horizon shrinks, and the partition becomes time-dependent: at each instant the exterior region grows --- it now contains the accumulated Hawking flux --- while the horizon's $x_4$-stationary mode count, and hence its area, decreases. What changes under evaporation is therefore *the location of the cut*, not the law that holds across it.

*Step 3 (monotonicity of the total forces the balance).* Write $S_{\mathrm{total}} = S_{\mathrm{ext}} + S_{\mathrm{BH}}$, the decomposition induced by the (now moving) partition of Step 2. By Step 1, $dS_{\mathrm{total}}/dt > 0$ at every instant, irrespective of how the partition moves. Hence
$$\frac{dS_{\mathrm{ext}}}{dt} \;+\; \frac{dS_{\mathrm{BH}}}{dt} \;=\; \frac{dS_{\mathrm{total}}}{dt} \;>\; 0 ,$$
which is the refined Generalized Second Law. As the hole evaporates, $S_{\mathrm{BH}}$ decreases monotonically with the area; therefore $S_{\mathrm{ext}}$ *must* increase by at least as much, and does. $\square$

**Remark 16.3.4.1 (why the balance is not a coincidence).** The content of Theorem 16.3.4 is best seen by asking what would have to be true for it to *fail*. It would have to be possible for the horizon to shed area faster than the outgoing radiation could carry entropy away --- that is, for the total entropy of the manifold to decrease over some interval of the evaporation. By Theorem 11 that is impossible, and impossible for a reason that has nothing to do with black holes: *$x_4$ advances and does not retreat*. The entropy exchange between hole and radiation therefore balances *because it must*, the global monotonicity of the $+ic$ advance permitting no other outcome.

This inverts the orthodox reading. There, the Generalized Second Law is a delicate bookkeeping identity that black holes happen to satisfy, established through thought-experiments and checked case by case, and its mechanism is obscure. Here it is a corollary of the same monotonic $x_4$-advance that gives the Second Law of thermodynamics for a cup of coffee. *Thermodynamics has not been extended, refined, or modified to accommodate the horizon --- it has only been partitioned differently.* The horizon is a cut in the manifold, not an exception to it.

**Remark 16.3.4.2 (the Generalized Second Law is Geometric Channel content, and could not be otherwise).** Theorem 16.3.4 descends from the $+ic$ orientation, and by Theorem 17-ter (the Content-Asymmetry Theorem) *no chain of reasoning conducted within the Algebraic Channel could have produced it*: the symmetry group of the coordinate label is sign-blind on $+ic$, and a law asserting that entropy increases is precisely a law that distinguishes $+ic$ from $-ic$. The Generalized Second Law is therefore not merely *derivable* along the Geometric Channel --- it is *only* derivable there. This is a structural prediction of Theorem 17-ter borne out in a specific theorem, and it is the reason the resolution of the information paradox in §16.4 requires *both* channels: the Algebraic Channel supplies the unitarity (a symmetry statement, blind to the arrow), and the Geometric Channel supplies the monotonicity (an orientation statement, invisible to the symmetries). Neither channel alone contains the paradox, and neither alone contains its resolution.

# 16.4 Part (c) of GR T22: The Structural Argument that the Dual-Channel Architecture Dissolves the Paradox {#sec:T22-C}

## 16.4.1 The category-error of the standard formulation

**Claim 16.4.1 (The information paradox is a category-error).** The standard formulation of the information paradox (Hawking 1976, Definition 16.1.1) implicitly assumes that the *macroscopic-observer thermal spectrum* and the *microscopic unitary evolution* are constraints on *the same structural object*. The McGucken framework shows that the two are constraints on *structurally different content* of $dx_4/dt = ic$: $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel (microscopic unitary, S-matrix level) and the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel (macroscopic coarse-grained, thermodynamic level).

The category-error in detail:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{4.8cm}p{4.5cm}p{4.5cm}}
\hline
\textbf{Aspect} & \textbf{Algebraic Channel (microscopic)} & \textbf{Geometric Channel (macroscopic)} \\
\hline
Physical content of $dx_4/dt = ic$ & Algebraic-symmetry: ISO(3), Stone's theorem, Noether currents, time-symmetric microscopic dynamics, unitary evolution $\hat U$ & Geometric-propagation: $+ic$ orientation, isotropic expansion, McGucken Sphere flow, $dS/dt > 0$ \\
\hline
Mathematical object & Bogoliubov S-matrix $\hat U_{\mathrm{Bog}}: \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}} \to \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{out}}$ & Hawking thermal density matrix $\hat\rho_{\mathrm{thermal}}$ at $T_H(t)$ \\
\hline
Information content & Pure-to-pure: information preserved & Pure-to-mixed (coarse-grained): information appears to be lost \\
\hline

\hline
